Headers differ: React shows “Settings” plus the “Channel #design” subtitle; Android shows only “Edit Channel” and omits the subtitle.
Pin controls differ: React has a “Preferences” heading, helper copy, and an off-state switch; Android omits these and shows a full-width outlined “Pin” action button.
Android omits the “Channel actions” heading and helper text. Its Name and Description fields are shorter, with heavier outlines; React's focused Name field has a double-ring treatment.
Cancel and Save differ in placement and state: Android places them below the fields with a disabled gray Save, while React places them at the bottom right with an active pink Save.
likelyCauses: The Android implementation uses a dialog component rather than React's full-screen panel component.
The Android feature specification omits or restructures the Preferences and Channel actions sections.
Component sizing and border-stroke tokens differ between the React and Android implementations.
Form state differs: Save is disabled and the Name field is not focused in the Android capture.
cases.suggestedOwner: Android channel-settings feature owner and design-system team
suggestedFixes: Use a full-screen 390×844 white panel on Android, removing the centered modal bounds, rounded outer corners, and dark scrim.
Match the React header by showing “Settings” and the “Channel #design” subtitle.
Restore the Preferences and Channel actions headings and helper copy; replace the standalone Pin button with the off-state switch.
Match React's field heights, border weight, corner radius, and focused Name-field outline, especially the taller Description textarea.
Move Cancel and Save into a bottom-right action area with the baseline divider, and reconcile Save's enabled state so visual state matches the actual form validity.

summary: Android uses a different component hierarchy: a green System permission banner, an On this device toggle card, and Workspace radio cards replace React's single Push Notifications configuration card.
Android adds multiple controls absent on React: notification permission status, four device-setting switches, a test-notification action, and All messages/Only mentions choices.
React's Unavailable badge, disabled Enable Push Notifications and Save buttons, and unchecked Mute this server checkbox are missing on Android.

Android's row headings are slightly smaller and lighter than React's bold headings, with denser body spacing; Android also uses brighter green/yellow state fills and thicker outlines than React's neutral gray styling.
The Android Only mentions card is cropped by the bottom of the viewport, while React's complete card remains visible with blank space below.
likelyCauses: The two implementations appear to use different screen specifications or information architectures.
Android-specific permission, toggle, and workspace states expose a different component set.
The platforms are using separate typography, spacing, color, and control-style tokens.
The Android page exceeds the fixed 390×844 capture area without sufficient scroll handling or bottom inset.
cases.suggestedOwner: Android Notifications UI team, with the cross-platform design-system owner
suggestedFixes: Choose a canonical structure and align Android to the React baseline, or explicitly update the baseline if the Android settings hierarchy is the intended design.
If React parity is required, restore the Push Notifications heading, Unavailable badge, explanatory text, disabled buttons, and Mute this server checkbox on Android.
Match the shared type scale and weights, particularly row titles and section headings, which are bold and larger in React but lighter and smaller in Android.
Align card shapes, radii, borders, margins, and state colors, including the yellow enabled switch and green selected workspace card versus React's subdued gray palette.
Add scrolling or bottom padding so the Only mentions card is fully visible, and use matching crop contracts for both snapshots.

summary: Android truncates the top-bar title to “Computer Missing Pr...”, shows a different subtitle, adds a chat icon, and uses horizontal overflow dots; React shows the full title and handle with vertical overflow dots.

The profile header differs in spacing and composition: Android adds top padding and a separate Display name row, omits the edit pencil and Codex CLI CPU icon, and shows a compact yellow “Working” status instead of React’s long truncated “Capturing deterministic profile sta...” status.
Description typography and bounds differ: Android uses smaller body text with different line wrapping and omits the pencil affordance next to the heading.

The Info section is a single vertical stack in React but a compact, partly two-column layout in Android. Android adds a purple Member chip, a standalone dash above “No computer assigned,” a side-by-side Creator, and a letter-based avatar.

Runtime Config is lower-case with a pencil and stacked plain values in React; Android uses title case, a two-column grid, colored value chips, and a visible Environment Variables row with truncated pill labels.

Toolbar actions, title constraints, and overflow-button orientation are configured independently.
Different fields or labels are mapped into the app-bar subtitle and profile status indicator.
Platform-specific typography, spacing, and density tokens have diverged from the React visual contract.
Icon mappings and field/chip templates differ, causing edit, CPU, avatar, and state treatments to change or disappear.
cases.suggestedOwner: Android UI/design-system team, aligned with the shared React profile specification
suggestedFixes: Align the app bar with React by fitting the full title, restoring the expected subtitle, using the same overflow orientation, and removing or consistently styling the extra chat action.
Match the profile-header spacing and content: avatar/detail alignment, title and subtitle, edit affordance, Codex CLI icon, Display name treatment, and status text/icon.
Use the shared Description heading and body typography, including the pencil affordance and expected line wrapping.
Match the Info field order, column structure, separators, Role and Creator treatments, and Computer value so the dash does not create an extra row.
Align Runtime Config capitalization, heading affordance, value/chip styling, spacing, and Environment Variables presentation; ensure the layout reaches the same visible controls at 390×844.

summary: Android shows a compact yellow “Working” badge, while React shows a wide truncated “Capturing deterministic profile sta…” status. Android also renders populated profile fields that React omits during loading.

Responsive spacing tokens differ around the profile hero.
Subtitle and field data fallbacks are inconsistent between implementations.

Align hero spacing and controls, including the name edit pencil and the Codex CLI chip icon.
Reconcile Info fields and ordering so Display name, Role value, Computer value, Created, and Creator render consistently in both platforms.
Use one Runtime Config layout and chip treatment, including heading capitalization, edit affordance, column arrangement, and chip colors.

summary: React shows an open “Change avatar” modal: a rounded white bottom sheet with a close X, divider, and disabled Save button. Android shows the undimmed profile page with no sheet.

React’s picker uses 4 large columns with category headings such as “Bot family,” “Critters,” “Space,” “Desk,” and “Food”; Android uses a dense 8-column grid under “Choose Avatar” without category headings.

React places upload in a separate dashed tile beside the current-avatar preview, while Android places upload first in the grid. Selection emphasis also changes from a yellow outline on React to a pink/red outline on Android.

Android exposes a large profile avatar and title, “Agent,” “Codex CLI,” and yellow “Working” badges, plus Display name and Description fields; these are not visible in React’s captured modal state. Android also adds a header chat bubble.
Typography and spacing differ: React uses a large bold modal title and roomy grouped sections, while Android uses smaller labels, tighter gaps, and more compact tiles.
likelyCauses: The captures represent different UI states: React is in an avatar-change modal while Android is on the underlying profile page.
The platforms use different avatar-grid specifications, including column count, tile size, gaps, and category grouping.
Avatar upload and selected-state styling are not implemented from a shared component.
The crop contracts differ: React uses component-bounds while Android uses manual viewport-bounds, reducing like-for-like comparison.
cases.suggestedOwner: Android avatar-management UI team with design-system support
suggestedFixes: Capture both platforms in the same state; either open the “Change avatar” sheet on Android or expose the React modal as the same inline picker.
Use identical grid tokens for columns, avatar dimensions, spacing, borders, and section headings.
Standardize the upload affordance and selected-avatar outline color, thickness, radius, and inset.
Align modal/picker typography and spacing, then include matching header actions, status badges, and editable-field labels in the compared state.
Use the same component or viewport crop contract for both screenshots before rerunning Slock.

Conditional state and plan-limit handling are not shared consistently between the React and Android implementations.

Do not expose the full form in the no-computer fixture, or update both platforms and snapshots to an explicitly approved shared state.
Make the Android form body scrollable with bottom padding for the footer, and ensure the Reasoning dropdown is never overlapped or cropped.
Add a matching cross-platform fixture for the Free-plan limit and no-computer conditions.
